repos.title: LEANN: A Low-Storage Vector Index
repos.paper_summary:
LEANN is a storage-efficient vector index that recomputes embeddings at query time instead of storing them, and prunes the proximity graph while keeping high-degree hub nodes. It builds on HNSW and FAISS. A two-level search uses approximate product-quantization (PQ) distances to select candidates for exact recomputation, and dynamic batching groups recomputations across exploration steps (target batch of 64) to improve GPU use. High-degree preserving pruning keeps the top 2% of nodes by degree at maximum degree M and caps other nodes at M/5.

On a 76 GB text corpus (RPJ-Wiki) with Qwen3-4B on an RTX 4090, LEANN uses 4 GB of storage versus 188 GB for HNSW and 20 GB for PQ. End-to-end RAG latency is 23.3 s for LEANN and 21.0 s for HNSW, with 25.5% downstream accuracy for both. Table 2 reports retrieval latency at 90% recall across NQ, GPQA, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA.

Limitations: search latency rises from milliseconds to seconds, which the paper accepts because generation dominates RAG latency. Some baselines (HNSW, IVF) ran on a larger-memory server.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Graph indices for a 76 GB corpus need 188 GB, too large for personal devices, so a smaller index is needed.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Proximity graph indices need few distance computations, but storage has two parts: vectors and index metadata.

digest_headlines.heading: LEANN Overview
digest_headlines.headline: LEANN keeps a pruned graph and product-quantized codes, recomputing exact embeddings during queries.

digest_headlines.heading: Graph-based Recomputation
digest_headlines.headline: Two-level search and dynamic batching cut recomputation while keeping exact distances for selected candidates.

digest_headlines.heading: Compact Graph Structure
digest_headlines.headline: Preserving edges of the top 2% high-degree nodes shrinks graph metadata while maintaining high retrieval accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Index Building and Update
digest_headlines.headline: Sharded construction and buffered updates limit peak storage during index building and modification.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: LEANN matches the accuracy of the standard graph index at 90% recall while storing about 5% of raw data size.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier systems reduce memory via disk layouts, quantization or online embedding but still store embeddings.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: LEANN keeps the index under 5% of raw data size, up to 50 times smaller than existing methods, with high recall.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers relative neighborhood graph pruning, update algorithms, Mac latency, and ablations on construction, embedding model, caching, and latency breakdown.

repos.title: SUPRA-TEX: 3D Generation with Super-Aligned Texture
repos.paper_summary: SUPRA-Tex generates relightable 3D assets with PBR materials from a single reference image, keeping the reference's text, logos, and patterns at their visible surface locations. A 2D model built on a multimodal DiT predicts albedo and metallic-roughness maps in the reference view in one forward pass, taking 1.2 s on one H800. These maps are projected onto visible surface voxels and encoded by the frozen pretrained material VAE encoder into observation latents, which carry coverage and boundary-distance metadata. An interleaved flow transformer then generates full-surface material latents with flow matching. Observation latents serve as fixed, read-only memory, and blocks alternate between updating unobserved cells and the full surface. The 2D estimator is trained on Objaverse renders. The paper reports the best results among the evaluated methods in geometry-conditioned texturing and end-to-end generation, but the provided Table 1 excerpt cuts off before the SUPRA-Tex row, so this summary gives no SUPRA-Tex scores. Stated limitations include errors from upstream geometry or 2D material estimation, inconsistent completion across visibility boundaries, and qualitative-only failure cases with no paired two-view result.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-view fusion and native 3D generation both lose fine reference details, motivating a split into material estimation, alignment and completion.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior texturing either fuses inconsistent multi-view predictions or conditions a native generator on implicit image features.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Method
digest_headlines.headline: SUPRA-Tex estimates reference-view PBR maps, encodes them as fixed observation anchors, and completes the full-surface material latents.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: SUPRA-Tex leads all shaded and PBR metrics in given-geometry texturing on both evaluation datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Errors in upstream geometry, 2D material estimates and unobserved regions limit fidelity and asset quality.

digest_headlines.heading: 6 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Trained only on public data, SUPRA-Tex reaches top results among evaluated methods and is competitive with commercial systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives training data, optimization, evaluation protocols, ablations, extra qualitative comparisons and a notation table.

repos.title: Raven: The Harness of Harnesses for Composable Agentic Intelligence
repos.paper_summary: Raven is an open-source multi-agent ecosystem that automatically constructs and orchestrates modular agent harnesses for long-horizon, cross-domain tasks. The Host Agent decomposes goals into subtasks, assigns them to specialized agents, and coordinates execution via a directed acyclic graph with explicit artifact dependencies. A diagnosis-driven evolution loop improves harness configurations by testing candidates against frozen task models, while Skill Forge retrieves reusable procedures from past executions. The paper establishes sufficient conditions under which composing multiple agents expands reliable task coverage beyond individual capabilities within a shared resource budget. On the new Multi-Agent Orchestration Benchmark (MAOB), Raven outperforms all baselines on four planning metrics using two backbone models, achieving Exact Match gains of 10.4 and 10.5 percentage points over the strongest competitor. Domain-specific evaluations show that native specialists perform competitively in research, coding, design, and operations. Experiments indicate that the curated skill library improves performance on three benchmarks, yielding larger gains than OpenClaw on two of them. The theoretical guarantees require specific compatibility conditions that may be difficult to verify for arbitrary third-party agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Raven composes model–harness agents through a host that plans, dispatches, and integrates work across domains.

digest_headlines.heading: Theory
digest_headlines.headline: Under a shared budget, sufficient conditions let composed agents reliably cover tasks that individual agents cannot reliably solve alone.

digest_headlines.heading: Multi-Agent Collaboration
digest_headlines.headline: A typed dependency graph is validated before dispatch, and every handoff passes through a recorded artifact.

digest_headlines.heading: Agent Harness Self-Evolution
digest_headlines.headline: Harness evolution edits a frozen model's strategy interfaces and keeps candidates only after paired screening.

digest_headlines.heading: Memory System
digest_headlines.headline: EverOS memory consolidates episodes into scenes and profiles, and Raven recalls them through hybrid retrieval.

digest_headlines.heading: Skill Forge
digest_headlines.headline: Skill Forge fuses skills from three sources, selects them through a gate, and revises skills from execution cases.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Raven ranks first on all four graph metrics under both backbones, with Exact Match gains of 10.4 and 10.5 percentage points.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans orchestration, harness evolution, agent memory, and skills, which Raven combines with explicit boundaries.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Raven's conclusion summarizes planning and skill results and proposes a multi-device network as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix contains notation, execution semantics, the finite-query limit, and details of benchmark, grading, and ablation protocols.

repos.title: YANchor-4B: Effective Long-Horizon Reasoning in O(N) Time with O(1) Memory
repos.paper_summary: EdgeRock is a family of multimodal reasoning models whose persistent history stays fixed in size however long the model reasons. Its first release, EdgeRock-4B, is converted from Qwen3.5-4B and adds Rock Memory Anchors (RMA). A learned writer produces a key-value record for each token, and a learned scorer rates it. Every 256 tokens, each of four KV groups keeps its 1,024 highest-scoring records from the committed bank and the new candidates. Queries read these records directly, alongside a 1,024-token sliding window and gated DeltaNet recurrent state. Attention KV is 72 MiB per sequence, versus 8 GiB for a 256K-token full-attention cache. On AIME 2024–2026, EdgeRock-4B reaches 82.9% mean pass@1, while the 16 bounded-state models evaluated, up to 14B parameters, reach at most 18.8%. Disabling RMA at inference lowers long-context query accuracy from 94.1% to 0.4%. Throughput is up to 6.42× that of Qwen3.5-4B on one 80GB GPU, measured at 32K input and 32K output with repeated prompts. Limitations: only the 4B model is released, and larger sizes are stated as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Growing reasoning caches strain serving and edge budgets, and bounded-state models lose reasoning, so EdgeRock adds learned fixed-size anchors.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 How is EdgeRock built?
digest_headlines.headline: EdgeRock-4B converts Qwen3.5-4B by replacing full attention with a 1,024-position window plus an RMA module in four training stages.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 How does RMA preserve distant information?
digest_headlines.headline: RMA keeps the highest-scoring records in a fixed bank of 1,024 per group, updated every 256 tokens, and any query can read them.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 What stays constant as context grows?
digest_headlines.headline: Persistent history per sequence stays fixed in size however long the model reasons, unlike a full-attention cache that grows with each token.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Evaluation design
digest_headlines.headline: The evaluation compares 28 models on 29 text benchmarks and measures visual reasoning, distant memory, and long-sequence inference.

digest_headlines.heading: 6 Does strong reasoning survive constant memory?
digest_headlines.headline: EdgeRock-4B reaches 82.9% on AIME 2024–2026 and retains 96.3% of its Qwen3.5-4B source's AIME mean.

digest_headlines.heading: 7 Do distant answers depend on RMA?
digest_headlines.headline: Disabling RMA at inference drops query accuracy from 94.1% to 0.4%, showing distant answers flow through the anchor bank.

digest_headlines.heading: 8 What does constant memory buy in deployment?
digest_headlines.headline: EdgeRock-4B runs 512 long-generation sequences at once on one accelerator and averages 4.94 times Qwen3.5-4B's end-to-end throughput.

digest_headlines.heading: 9 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed history makes memory a design-time property, which the authors argue lets robots, chips, and agents plan capacity before reasoning.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the text and visual evaluation protocols, bounded-state and compact benchmark tables, runtime tables, and the state-ownership specification.

repos.title: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness
repos.paper_summary:
Prime Agent is an open-source harness for long-horizon evaluation and coding-agent workflows. It provides a persistent IPython REPL, recursive subagents with direct agent-to-agent communication, and Continual Harness for storing versioned prompts, memories, skills, and subagent specifications across trajectories. The model controls strategy construction while the runtime standardizes execution, recovery, and resource accounting.

The paper evaluates Prime Agent against native and alternative harnesses (Pi, Claude Code, Codex) on interactive reasoning, long-context tasks, and autonomous systems construction. On ARC-AGI-3, Prime Agent raises RHAE Best@1 from 30% to 95.5%. In long-context benchmarks, it matches or exceeds baselines; for example, on OOLONG (Yahoo, 128k), GPT-5.6 Sol scores .940 with Prime Agent versus .900 with Codex. For GPU kernel generation on PMPP-Hard, Prime Agent achieves comparable solve rates at substantially reduced token cost. A seven-day Factorio run completed 24 of 196 technologies using 23.4 million output tokens. Limitations include models' poor handling of irreversible actions and online refinement potentially preserving specification exploits as reusable skills.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent argues the harness should expose expressive primitives, so evaluation measures model capability rather than harness failures.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Prime Agent Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent splits information management from computation management across persistent sessions, a daemon and Continual Harness state.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent is generally competitive on long-context tasks and close to native harnesses on GPU-kernel generation.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work spans programmatic inference, coding-agent runtimes, ARC-AGI-3 systems and multi-agent communication, which Prime Agent combines.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Many harness capabilities remain underused because current models were not trained to operate them.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists three out-of-loop nanoGPT experiments, from Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Pro and a third model, plus an orchestration example.

repos.title: Breaking the Space Barrier and its Application to Language Model Inference
repos.paper_summary:
*stcon* is a constrained-decoding engine for language models that applies constructions from a complexity-theory result on few-path graphs. The paper shows that deciding whether such a graph connects a source to a target is in ReachUL, LOGDCFL, C=L and SC2, using O(log²n / log log n) space, below Savitch's O(log²n) bound. For decoding, the token mask is recomputed on the GPU at each step instead of stored as a table, forced text is appended within the same model run, and independent JSON fields are decoded in parallel and verified against the model.

On one 16 GB Apple M2 Pro with Qwen3.5-2B and 4B (4-bit, greedy decoding), against MLX with llguidance, six JSON extractions finish in 1.89 s versus 2.41 s on the 2B and 3.89 s versus 4.59 s on the 4B. On the 2B, outputs match character for character. A 1,106-state tool-call grammar costs 3.4 MB instead of an 824 MB token table. Sixteen tool-calling agents finish in 29.3 s versus 74.6 s. Limitations: one machine and one model family, greedy decoding only, recursive grammars served one request at a time, and parallel decoding saves model runs but not wall time.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Constrained decoding adds per-step cost on a laptop, and this paper links it to a complexity question about few-path graphs.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: A laptop run is dominated by reading weights, and few-path graphs are defined as those with at most k walks between vertices.

digest_headlines.heading: The theory in plain words
digest_headlines.headline: Three ideas (budgets, certified fingerprints, one zero test) show total few-path reachability lies in ReachUL and related classes.

digest_headlines.heading: From the theory to the decoding engine
digest_headlines.headline: The decoding step graph is a tree, which yields six mechanisms for masks, forced text, budgets and parallel fields.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Six JSON extractions take 1.89 s on the 2B model against 2.41 s for MLX with llguidance, with the same answers.

digest_headlines.heading: Related work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers few-path complexity results and constrained-decoding libraries, and speculative decoding.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper expects the gains on memory-bound devices, but tests cover one machine, one model family and greedy decoding.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that the same constructions settle few-path reachability and make structured decoding cheaper.

digest_headlines.heading: Statement of novelty
digest_headlines.headline: The author states the theory was obtained independently and the remaining time went to the practical engine.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers background, formal theory and proofs, the implementation, all measurements, negative results and tests.

repos.title: StreamEval: Evaluating Interactive Streaming Video Generation Models
repos.paper_summary: StreamEval is a benchmark for interactive streaming video generation, covering five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing. It contains 300 scripted test cases of 15–300 s, each with initial assets, timed multimodal requests, and explicit requirements for state changes and content preservation. Ten task-specific metrics on a 0–100 scale cover four dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination. Construction uses model-assisted authoring with automated and VLM-based screening, and judges are calibrated against stated false-positive and false-negative thresholds. Across 37 models, the highest task-specific scores are 36.90 for Following among seven avatar-performance models, 25.93 for Following in text-conditioned world generation, and 15.00 for Edit Success among three reference-editing models. The authors report that high visual quality and identity retention do not reliably coincide with request execution or state consistency. Limitations stated include that human judgments have not yet been collected to check agreement with the rubric, and that the editing tables show only configurations with Overall at least 5, a subset chosen after evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: StreamEval introduces a 300-case benchmark spanning five interactive streaming video tasks with ten metrics.

digest_headlines.heading: The StreamEval Benchmark
digest_headlines.headline: Each case pairs timed user inputs with explicit execution and preservation criteria, balanced across five durations.

digest_headlines.heading: System Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Evaluating 38 models across five tasks, Vidu S2 Editing ranks first in both editing tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Analysis and Qualitative Results
digest_headlines.headline: A recorded reference-editing session shows retained source content but no adoption of the requested gold satin cape.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks each cover part of streaming video, leaving no single protocol for all five StreamEval task types.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Request execution and reference-based editing remain challenging, with the highest reference Edit Success at 15.00.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the StreamEval team, notes that author order does not reflect contributions, and acknowledges partners.

repos.title: OpenGCUA: Toward a Fully Open Stack for Generalist Computer Use
repos.paper_summary:
OpenGCUA is the first release of an ongoing project to open the full stack for generalist computer-use agents (GCUAs), which choose at each step what to observe, how to act, and how to organize work across GUI, accessibility-tree, shell, and API interfaces. The release includes the implementation, prompts, trajectories from eight frontier models, and preliminary real-device harness and cross-device SDK. It does not include a newly trained model.

The paper studies two mechanisms. Code execution has the model write one Python program per step that combines PyAutoGUI calls, `bash()` shell commands, and control flow, so intermediate results can determine later operations without another model call. Harness-to-model decision transfer lets the model decide when to request screenshots and how to track task state.

On the offline OSWorld-v2 set, the full configuration raises mean partial score by 19.6 points across all eight models and cuts steps per task by 53.0% relative to batched GUI-only execution. Against a GUI+CLI baseline, code execution adds 6.1 points and cuts steps by 14.8%. On four real macOS tasks, Qwen3.8-Max uses 19.4 times as many reasoning tokens as GPT-6 Astra. The authors state that the harness and SDK remain preliminary.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Open Generalist computer-use agent project releases agent designs, evaluation trajectories and preliminary tools, without a trained model.

digest_headlines.heading: Generalist CUA: Definition and Positioning
digest_headlines.headline: A generalist computer-use agent is defined by three per-step decisions: what to observe, how to act, and how to organize work.

digest_headlines.heading: Agent Design: Code Execution and Harness-to-Model Decision Transfer
digest_headlines.headline: Code execution and model-requested screenshots are tested on OSWorld-v2 with gains in task score and cache reuse for selected models.

digest_headlines.heading: Real-Device Generalist CUA
digest_headlines.headline: On four real macOS tasks, Qwen3.8-Max averages 50.2K reasoning tokens per task against 2.6K for GPT-6 Astra under one harness.

digest_headlines.heading: Roadmap
digest_headlines.headline: The next release is planned to add a trained generalist computer-use model, with work on efficient reasoning and real-device benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing open computer-use models focus on graphical interfaces, while hybrid graphical-and-programmatic systems are only beginning to appear.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Across eight models, the full configuration raises mean partial score by 19.6 points on the offline OSWorld-v2 subset.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists evaluation details, real-device task descriptions, the prompts, and trajectory examples from GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.

repos.title: LeRobot: An Open-Source Library for End-to-End Robot Learning
repos.paper_summary:
`lerobot` is an open-source Python library for end-to-end robot learning that integrates low-level motor control, data collection, and policy training. It supports eight hardware platforms, including the SO-100 and ALOHA-2, using a shared middleware API for teleoperation. The library introduces `LeRobotDataset`, a standardized format for multimodal robotics data that enables streaming large datasets without full downloads. As of September 2025, the ecosystem includes over 16,000 datasets from 2,200 contributors.

The library provides PyTorch implementations of leading algorithms such as ACT, Diffusion Policy, $\pi_{0}$, and SmolVLA. Inference benchmarks on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 show ACT achieving 5.01 ms latency, while the larger $\pi_{0}$ model requires 209 ms. An asynchronous inference stack decouples action prediction from execution, allowing policies to run on remote machines. Limitations include incomplete coverage of robot embodiments and algorithms, and the lack of low-level optimizations like quantization or graph compilation for practical deployment.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Robot learning tools are fragmented, so the authors present lerobot, an open-source library spanning the full stack from motor control to datasets.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Low-cost open arms cost a fraction of industrial ones, and this accessibility supports decentralized data collection.

digest_headlines.heading: Features
digest_headlines.headline: lerobot supports several low-cost arms, a shared dataset format with 16K+ datasets, and reference implementations of policies.

digest_headlines.heading: Simulation
digest_headlines.headline: Simulation is used only for benchmarking, since the authors find simulation challenging for the contact-rich tasks the library targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: lerobot is presented as a unified open stack, with limits in robot coverage, algorithm count, and inference optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists robot build guides, dataset breakdowns, the streaming dataset design, model and inference examples, and a synchronous versus asynchronous comparison.

repos.title: Fish Audio S2 Technical Report
repos.paper_summary: Fish Audio S2 is an open-source text-to-speech system that uses a Dual-Autoregressive architecture to generate multi-speaker audio with natural-language control. The model employs a Qwen3-4B backbone for semantic token prediction and a 4-layer network for acoustic detail reconstruction. Training involves a data pipeline that filters audio using a speech quality model and generates rich transcriptions via an ASR model, which are reused as reward signals during Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training. On the Seed-TTS-Eval benchmark, Fish Audio S2 achieves a Word Error Rate of 0.54% in Chinese and 0.99% in English, outperforming CosyVoice 3-1.5B (1.12% and 2.21%, respectively). In production on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU, the system reaches a Real-Time Factor of 0.195 and a time-to-first-audio latency of 100 ms. Evaluation on the Emergent TTS Eval shows an 81.88% win rate against a baseline. A limitation is that performance lags behind MiniMax Speech and ElevenLabs in low-resource languages with under 1,000 hours of training data.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-grained speech control lacks training data at scale, so the report pairs a data pipeline with reinforcement-learning alignment.

digest_headlines.heading: Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: The codec is streaming-capable, and generation splits a slow semantic model from a fast 4-layer acoustic model.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Pipeline
digest_headlines.headline: Three-stage pipeline separates vocals, filters with a speech quality model, and annotates speech with a rich-transcription model, whose outputs also serve as rewards.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Training runs in four stages, from a 446-million-parameter tokenizer through over 10 million hours of pre-training to reinforcement-learning post-training.

digest_headlines.heading: Inference Engine
digest_headlines.headline: Streaming inference built on SGLang reaches an RTF of 0.195 and first audio in as little as 100 ms on one high-end accelerator.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Fish Audio S2 reports the lowest error rate on Chinese and English voice-cloning benchmarks and in 11 of 24 languages on the multilingual testset.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The report concludes that its architecture, dual-purpose data pipeline and multi-reward RL support controllable, multi-speaker speech, and that weights and code are released.

digest_headlines.heading: Author
digest_headlines.headline: Core contributors are ranked by contribution, and the other contributors are shuffled with a fixed seed.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix describes the Fish Audio Instruction Benchmark's construction, Gemini 3 Pro judging metrics, and its human-agreement checks.
